title: Notation
summary: VIO state, coordinate frames, and rigid-body coordinate transformations.

content.text: Visual–inertial odometry (VIO) combines camera and inertial measurements to estimate the metric six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) motion of a sensing platform: three-dimensional position and orientation. Images constrain motion through observations of the surrounding scene, while IMU measurements constrain motion between image timestamps.

We describe the platform motion using three coordinate frames: the global frame \(\{G\}\), the IMU frame \(\{I\}\), and the camera frame \(\{C\}\). The global frame provides the coordinates in which we express the estimated trajectory; the IMU and camera frames move with their respective sensors.

content.alt: Global frame G, rigidly mounted IMU frame I and camera frame C, and a fixed environment point f. A blue connector denotes the IMU pose; dotted lines indicate point positions and visual observation.
content.caption: Global, IMU, and camera frames. The camera and IMU form a rigid sensor platform. The blue connector denotes a pose relation, not a trajectory. Dotted lines relate the same environment point \(f\) to the frames.

Here, \({}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I}\) and \({}^{G}\mathbf{v}_{I}\) are the IMU position and velocity expressed in the global frame. The rotation matrix \({}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R}\) maps vector coordinates from the global frame into the IMU frame. The vectors \(\mathbf{b}_{g}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_{a}\) are the gyroscope and accelerometer biases. Velocity and biases are estimated alongside pose because they affect the integration of inertial measurements.

The frame labels specify how each quantity should be read. For a position, the superscript identifies the frame in which its coordinates are expressed, and the subscript identifies the object. Thus, \({}^{G}\mathbf{p}_{I}\) is the position of the IMU origin expressed in \(\{G\}\). For a rotation, the lower frame label is the source and the upper label is the destination.

Subtracting the IMU position first expresses the point relative to the IMU origin; the rotation then expresses that displacement along the IMU axes.

A rigid-body coordinate transformation combines rotation and translation in one matrix. We write \({}^{A}_{B}\mathbf{T}\) for the transform that maps point coordinates from frame \(\{B\}\) into frame \(\{A\}\). Appending a 1 to a three-dimensional point gives its homogeneous coordinates. These operations change how the same point is expressed in different frames.

The camera–IMU extrinsic transform \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{T}\) maps IMU coordinates into camera coordinates. Its rotation block is \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{R}\), and its translation block is the IMU origin expressed in \(\{C\}\). For rigidly mounted sensors, this transform is constant. title: Camera and IMU measurement models
summary: Image projection, gyroscope angular rate, and accelerometer specific force.

content.text: A camera records an array of pixel intensities or colors at each image timestamp. Feature detection and tracking extract two-dimensional point coordinates from these images. A projection model relates those coordinates to the three-dimensional geometry viewed by the camera. We use point coordinates as a representative observation; direct methods can instead compare image intensities.

Let \({}^{C}\mathbf{p}_f=(X,Y,Z)^\top\) denote an environment point expressed in the camera frame. We take the camera's optical axis as \(+Z_C\), with \(X_C\) pointing right and \(Y_C\) down in the image. For an ideal pinhole camera with known intrinsics, zero skew, and no lens distortion, its observed pixel coordinates \(\mathbf{z}_f=(u,v)^\top\) follow:

The focal lengths \(f_x,f_y\) and principal-point coordinates \(c_x,c_y\) are expressed in pixels. The principal point is where the optical axis meets the ideal image plane. The point coordinates \(X,Y,Z\) use a common length unit; in VIO we express them in meters. Here \(Z\) is depth along the optical axis. The term \(\mathbf{n}_c\) represents error in the extracted pixel coordinates, not noise in pixel intensity. This example assumes ideal or undistorted observations.

content.alt: A camera center and a virtual image plane. One viewing ray passes through a blue image observation and two hollow candidate positions at different depths. Both candidate positions have the same ideal projection.
content.caption: One image coordinate, multiple possible depths. The hollow points \({}^{C}\mathbf{p}_f\) and \(\lambda\,{}^{C}\mathbf{p}_f\), with \(\lambda>1\), are alternative positions consistent with the same ideal observation \(\mathbf{z}_f\). The virtual image plane is drawn in front of the camera center. Measurement noise is omitted in this schematic \(\left(\mathbf{n}_c=\mathbf{0}\right)\).

content.text: Projection divides by depth. Multiplying all three point coordinates by the same positive factor leaves their ratios unchanged:

Thus, under this calibrated model, a single point observation determines a viewing ray, but does not determine the point's distance along it. The two hollow locations in the figure show different possible depths for one observation. Additional views or other information are needed to resolve that ambiguity.

The camera pose determines a fixed environment point's coordinates in \(\{C\}\) and therefore its predicted projection. Observations of fixed points across images provide constraints on camera motion and scene geometry. The transform between camera and IMU coordinates is described in

An IMU provides timestamped, three-axis gyroscope and accelerometer readings, rather than direct orientation, velocity, or position measurements. We use an additive model with scale and axis errors assumed corrected or negligible. Readings are expressed along the common IMU axes. We neglect Earth rotation, treat \(\{G\}\) as locally inertial, and assume constant gravity.
The gyroscope measures angular velocity, which describes how orientation changes over time. Its measurement model is

Here \({}^{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is the IMU's angular velocity relative to \(\{G\}\), expressed along the IMU axes. Its direction gives the instantaneous rotation axis under the right-hand rule, and its magnitude gives angular speed; neither specifies the current orientation. The vectors \(\mathbf{b}_g\) and \(\mathbf{n}_g\) are bias and measurement noise. All terms have units of radians per second. For the global-to-IMU rotation \({}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R}\),

A dot denotes a time derivative, and \([\mathbf{u}]_{\times}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\) defines the cross-product matrix. The minus sign follows the global-to-IMU coordinate convention. Integration requires an initial orientation relative to the chosen \(\{G\}\); the gyroscope does not supply it. Integrating the three components independently does not generally give roll, pitch, and yaw.

Bias and noise play different roles. We model bias as an unknown offset that may change slowly, and noise as zero-mean random measurement error. An estimator subtracts an estimated bias before integration; the true bias and individual noise samples remain unknown. Bias errors and noise both affect the integrated state. Zero-mean noise need not cancel over a finite interval.
The accelerometer measures specific force, the non-gravitational force per unit mass acting on the sensor. Its measurement model is

Here \({}^{G}\mathbf{a}_I=d({}^{G}\mathbf{v}_I)/dt\) is the IMU origin's motion acceleration and \({}^{G}\mathbf{g}\) is gravitational acceleration, both expressed in \(\{G\}\). The reading \(\mathbf{a}_m\), bias \(\mathbf{b}_a\), and noise \(\mathbf{n}_a\) use IMU axes and have units of meters per second squared, as do the global acceleration terms. The same bias/noise distinction applies to both sensors.

Rotating the bias-corrected reading into \(\{G\}\) with \(({}^{I}_{G}\mathbf{R})^\top\) and adding gravity gives an acceleration estimate. An incorrect tilt can produce apparent motion acceleration even at rest. Velocity and position then require time integration and their initial values.

For a stationary, bias-free, noiseless sensor with aligned global and IMU axes and \(+z\) upward, \({}^{G}\mathbf{a}_I=\mathbf{0}\) and \({}^{G}\mathbf{g}=(0,0,-g)^\top\), with \(g>0\). Its accelerometer reads \((0,0,g)^\top\): the table supports it against gravity. In ideal, non-rotating free fall it reads zero, even though the sensor accelerates under gravity.

title: Camera–IMU calibration and synchronization
summary: Camera and IMU calibration parameters, sensor synchronization, and calibration procedures.

content.text: Section 2.1 assumed known focal lengths and principal-point coordinates, with lens distortion absent or already removed. Camera calibration determines these parameters for a chosen projection model. Real lenses can displace image points from their ideal pinhole positions. This displacement depends on image location and should be distinguished from random error in locating a feature.
For a pinhole camera with a lens-distortion model, we write

Here, \(\mathbf{z}_f\) is a feature coordinate in the original, distorted image, and \(\mathbf{d}\) contains the coefficients of the selected distortion model. The projection \(\pi\) now includes this distortion. For this model, \(\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}\) recovers the ideal projection in Section 2.1. Other camera models use different parameterizations.

content.alt: One image-coordinate plane with u pointing right and v pointing down. Hollow circles mark ideal pinhole locations. Blue filled circles mark their distorted locations in a radial barrel-distortion example. Thin arrows point from each ideal location toward its distorted counterpart, with larger displacements farther from the principal point.
content.caption: A radial-distortion example. Each arrow maps an ideal pinhole location (hollow circle) to its distorted location (blue dot) on the same pixel coordinate plane. The displacement grows with distance from the principal point \((c_x,c_y)\) in this example. This is a schematic mapping, not measured calibration data; random measurement noise is omitted.

content.text: One common calibration method observes a target with known geometry from several positions and orientations. The solver estimates camera parameters that explain the detected target points across images. It also estimates the target pose relative to the camera in each image: knowing the target geometry does not make these poses known. Views that cover different image regions and inclinations provide more useful constraints than repeated central, front-facing views.

The parameters must match the images used by the estimator. Original distorted images require the corresponding distortion model; undistorted images require the output camera model and should not be distorted again in prediction. Resizing scales focal lengths and principal-point coordinates; cropping shifts the principal point. These updates must follow the actual pixel-coordinate mapping. A known resize does not automatically require recalibration. Focus or lens-setting changes may require new parameters.
Section 2.2 assumed that IMU scale and axis errors were corrected or negligible. To describe these errors, consider a simplified model for the reported three-axis readings:

Here, \(\mathbf{s}\) is the true angular velocity or specific force expressed in the chosen IMU frame, and \(\mathbf{y}\) is the corresponding reported reading, in the same physical units. The dimensionless matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) describes scale and axis errors; \(\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{raw}}\) and \(\mathbf{n}_{\mathrm{raw}}\) are additive bias and noise in the reported readings. The gyroscope and accelerometer generally have different calibration matrices.

A scale error changes the response in proportion to the input. For example, a noise-free gyro with a 2% gain error and zero bias reports 1.02 rad/s for a true rate of 1 rad/s, and 2.04 rad/s for 2 rad/s. A bias adds an offset: 0.02 rad/s can remain even when the true rate is zero. One fixed bias correction therefore cannot remove the gain error at every rate. Misaligned or nonorthogonal sensing axes and cross-axis sensitivity can mix components; a nominal x-axis reading can respond to motion about another axis. These effects are distinct from the camera–IMU mounting rotation.

Intrinsic calibration identifies or verifies these scale and axis corrections. For invertible \(\mathbf{M}\), applying \(\mathbf{M}^{-1}\) to the readings also maps bias and noise into the corrected axes. Factory corrections may already be applied, so the actual output convention must be checked before applying another correction. Corrected gyro and accelerometer readings must use the same IMU axes as the camera–IMU extrinsic transform. The biases \(\mathbf{b}_g,\mathbf{b}_a\) in Section 2.2 are expressed in those corrected axes. They can change during operation and are often estimated with the navigation state; a calibration-time bias estimate is not necessarily valid for every later run.

Noise parameters describe statistical variation, rather than a correction to subtract from each sample. In the common white-noise and bias-random-walk model, measurement-noise density describes rapid fluctuations; a bias random-walk parameter describes the assumed strength of changes in bias over time. Neither is the current bias value. Gyroscope noise density, for example, can have units \((\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s})/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\), whereas a sampled reading has units rad/s. Converting density to sample variance depends on sampling and filtering assumptions.

Applicable sensor specifications or stationary recordings can help determine noise parameters. Allan deviation examines how fluctuations change with averaging time and can help fit the selected stochastic model. A stationary average can estimate gyro bias under the assumptions of Section 2.2, but an accelerometer also measures the gravity-related specific force at rest; its mean is not simply its bias. Parameter values must match the sensor settings, units, and model used by the estimator.

Camera–IMU extrinsics describe the relative orientation and position of the two sensors. A rigid mounting makes this physical relationship constant; it does not make its calibrated estimate exact. These parameters are distinct from the sensing-axis corrections in Section 3.2 and the platform's changing global pose. Following Section 1.2, \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{T}\) maps IMU point coordinates into camera coordinates:

Here, \({}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{f}\) comes from the scene geometry and IMU pose, not an IMU point measurement. The rotation \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{R}\) describes the IMU-axis directions relative to the camera axes: its columns are the IMU unit axes expressed in \(\{C\}\). Applying it re-expresses coordinates; it does not rotate the physical platform. The translation \({}^{C}\mathbf{p}_{I}\) points from the camera origin to the IMU origin, expressed in camera coordinates, in meters. Setting \({}^{I}\mathbf{p}_{f}=\mathbf{0}\) leaves exactly this translation.
For the reverse mapping, the rotation is \(\left({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{R}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\), and the translation is the camera origin expressed in IMU coordinates:
The opposite displacement must also be expressed in different axes, so changing its sign alone is generally insufficient.

The resulting \({}^{C}\mathbf{p}_{f}\) enters the camera projection model. Incorrect extrinsics can change the predicted image location even when the IMU pose and scene point are correct. Re-expressing the same direction vector uses only the rotation. Gyroscope and accelerometer readings are not point positions: rotating an accelerometer vector changes its expression axes, not the physical location where it was measured.

Calibration estimates this fixed transform from images and inertial measurements of the same moving platform. In a representative approach, the platform views a stationary target of known geometry. Images constrain camera poses; gyroscope and accelerometer data constrain angular velocity and specific force through Section 2.2's models. Rotation is constrained by agreement between image-inferred orientation changes and the inertial rotation model. Translation affects how the separated sensor origins move, particularly during rotation. In this approach, motion and biases are estimated together with the transform to explain both measurement streams, rather than treating either sensor's trajectory as known. Not every motion provides enough information to determine all extrinsic parameters.

When using calibration parameters, check the mapping direction, translation units, and sensor axes. Kalibr's \(\texttt{T\_cam\_imu}\) matches our \({}^{C}_{I}\mathbf{T}\). Invert the complete transform when the reverse direction is required, and use the corrected IMU axes from Section 3.2. Data collection and validation will be discussed in Section 3.5.
